name: Elena Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Elena, thank you for coming. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, so no AI companies, employers, unions or parties behind us, and nothing you say will have your name on it. You can tell me what you'd say to people and also what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All right. I'll be honest, I don't really know much about computers and AI, so I hope I'm the right person. But I know my own life well enough.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: That's exactly what I'm after. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Gerry Doyle, a small builder in town, him, his son Conor and me, doing house extensions and loft conversions. I'm the labourer and I'm learning carpentry from Gerry, so I mix the mortar, carry the joists up the scaffold, and lately he's had me cutting the noggins, the little bits of wood between the joists. Before this I was sixteen years at the supermarket on the high street, till and stockroom, until they put in the self-checkouts and cut my hours to nothing. I like that you finish a job and a family has an extra bedroom. What wears me out is the ladders, and Gerry's radio, which only plays one station.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there you go, all that fuss for nothing. People would be relieved, I think, and they'd go back to complaining about the price of bread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means I get to keep learning from Gerry, and maybe in a few years I'm a proper carpenter. That's all I want, a trade that's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on exactly as now, turn up at half seven, learn what Gerry shows me. Maybe ask him about doing the carpentry certificate at the college, if he'd let me have the Friday off. I wouldn't change anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Calm. It's the world I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the self-checkouts. How did that go for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It wasn't one big day, it was little cuts. First they took me off the till, then they cut my hours from thirty to twenty to twelve. By the end I was in the stockroom four mornings a week watching the machines beep at customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a month look like, money-wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight. Sam works at the big warehouse out by the ring road, picking orders, and between the two of us we cover the mortgage and the food and the kids' bus passes. If something breaks, the car or the fridge, it's a loan from my mother, and I hate asking.

S0.say: Well, there you go, all that fuss for nothing. People would be relieved and go back to complaining about the price of bread.
S0.think: It means I get to keep learning from Gerry and maybe become a proper carpenter in a few years. That's all I want, a trade that's mine.
S0.do: Carries on exactly as now, arriving at half past seven and learning carpentry from Gerry. Might ask him for Fridays off to do the carpentry certificate at the local college.
S0.feel: Calm, because it's the world she knows.
S0.quote: By the end I was in the stockroom four mornings a week watching the machines beep at customers.
S0.fieldNote: She has already lost hours to self-checkouts, but she tells it flatly, as just the way things went. In the calm picture her only goal is to have a trade of her own. She leans on her mother when bills come, which she clearly finds hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people will adjust, they always do. There'll be the usual shouting on both sides, the ones who say it's the end of the world and the ones who say it's wonderful, and the truth will be somewhere in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm a bit worried, but mostly for Sam. Gerry's jobs are small and fiddly, an old house where nothing is square, and I can't see a robot up our scaffold on Elm Street. The big sites, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't do much at first, honestly. I'd keep my head down, keep learning, and watch what happens to the big firms. If Gerry started talking about machines, I'd listen, but I wouldn't go near them until I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when you hear a noise downstairs at night and you lie there deciding whether to get up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the small jobs might be safe. What makes you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every house we do is different. Last month the old wall was leaning about three inches out and Gerry had to work out the roof by eye, more or less. A machine would want everything straight, and nothing in this town is straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Sam's job at the warehouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one that keeps me up. They've already got robots moving the shelves there, and Sam says they've stopped hiring for the night shift. If Sam loses that job, my wage covers maybe half the mortgage.

S1.say: People will adjust, they always do. There'll be shouting on both sides, the doom and the hype, and the truth will be somewhere in the middle.
S1.think: I'm a bit worried, but mostly for Sam at the warehouse. Gerry's jobs are small and fiddly, and I can't see a robot up our scaffold on an old house where nothing is square.
S1.do: Keeps her head down and keeps learning while watching what happens at the bigger firms. Listens if Gerry talks about machines but avoids them until she has no choice.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing a noise downstairs at night and deciding whether to get up.
S1.quote: A machine would want everything straight, and nothing in this town is straight.
S1.fieldNote: She takes comfort in the oddness of old houses and the small scale of Gerry's firm. Her real worry is her partner's warehouse job, where robots are already in use. Her natural response to change is to wait and watch rather than act.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it, at first. Then I'd say somebody, government, the companies, somebody, needs to sort it out, because you can't just switch off everyone's job at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd lose everything. Sam and me both doing jobs a robot can do, no savings, and nothing else round here. I'm forty-three and I didn't finish school, who's going to take me on for something new?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut everything straight away, the phone contracts, Ruby's dance class, the car if we can manage on the bus. Talk to my mother about moving in with her, because she's got the spare rooms. Go to the council and ask what help there is, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like drowning. Honestly, I don't think I'd cope very well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change, compared with the slower picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is no time. With the slow one, I could hide in Gerry's little jobs for a while, but if robots can do hands-on work in two years, there's nowhere to hide. I can't learn computers in two years, I can barely work the parking machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sell before the bank takes it, I suppose, and go to my mother's flat over the bakery. Four of us and her in three rooms. Kofi would have to change schools and he's only just made friends.

S2.say: I don't believe it, at first. Then I'd say somebody, government or the companies, needs to sort it out, because you can't switch off everyone's job at once.
S2.think: I think we'd lose everything, with Sam and me both doing jobs a robot can do and no savings. I'm forty-three and didn't finish school, so who's going to take me on for something new?
S2.do: Cuts phone contracts, her daughter's dance class and possibly the car straight away. Asks her mother about moving the family into her flat, sells the house before the bank can take it, and goes to the council for help for the first time.
S2.feel: Like drowning, and she doubts she would cope.
S2.quote: I can't learn computers in two years, I can barely work the parking machine.
S2.fieldNote: Both household incomes are exposed, there are no savings and no local alternatives, and she has no appetite for new technology. That combination leaves her without options in the fast picture. Moving in with her mother and her son changing schools came up as practical facts, not fears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, at least we've got a bit of warning. People should start getting ready, and the government should be thinking about what happens to all of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's still bad, just slower. Five years means Ruby's through school, which helps. But I'd still be the one who can't do the new stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving whatever I could, maybe forty a month, and cut back where we can. I'd stay with Gerry as long as he's working. I'd wait to see what the government does before doing anything big, because I don't want to throw money at the wrong thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but a slower kind of scared. More of a worry that sits on your chest all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years of warning, what would you do while you see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every month a bit more in the tin. No holiday, second-hand school uniforms, Sam doing overtime while there's overtime. We'd try to pay off my mother's loan for the car, so at least we're not owing family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning something new, with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If somebody showed me, step by step, like Gerry does. But I'm not going to sit in front of a computer on my own at night, I'd just get frustrated and give up. I know myself.

S3.say: At least we've got a bit of warning. People should start getting ready, and the government should be thinking about what happens to all of us.
S3.think: It's still bad, just slower. Five years means Ruby's through school, which helps, but I'd still be the one who can't do the new stuff.
S3.do: Saves about 40 a month and cuts back by skipping holidays and buying second-hand uniforms. Stays with Gerry as long as there's work and waits to see what the government does before any big step.
S3.feel: Scared in a slower way, a worry that sits on her chest all day.
S3.quote: I'm not going to sit in front of a computer on my own at night, I'd just get frustrated and give up. I know myself.
S3.fieldNote: Five years helps mostly because her older child would be finished with school. She would learn only if someone taught her in person, step by step, as Gerry does. She is honest about her limits without being bitter, and doesn't blame anyone in particular.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, things could change, and maybe it won't happen at all. I'd say let's not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years feels a bit better. Kofi would be twenty-one, the mortgage would be smaller, and Gerry's talking about retiring around then anyway. But I'd still be fifty-three with no qualifications.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working with Gerry, maybe get the carpentry certificate if he lets me have Fridays. Save a bit every month. Mostly I'd wait and see, because ten years is a long time and things could go differently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I could live with it. I'd probably push it to the back of my mind most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be fifty-three by 2036. What does ten years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means my kids are grown, and that's the big thing. If it was just me and Sam, we could manage in a smaller place. It's the kids that make it frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should be responsible for helping people like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of everyone. The government, the companies making the robots, and us too, to be honest. I don't think anyone owes me a living, but I don't think I should be thrown on the heap either.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time, things could change, and maybe it won't happen at all. Let's not panic.
S4.think: Ten years feels a bit better, with Kofi grown and the mortgage smaller. But I'd still be fifty-three with no qualifications, and Gerry will probably have retired.
S4.do: Keeps working with Gerry and may get the carpentry certificate if he allows Fridays off. Saves a little each month but mostly waits to see how things develop.
S4.feel: Worried but able to live with it, pushing it to the back of her mind most days.
S4.quote: I don't think anyone owes me a living, but I don't think I should be thrown on the heap either.
S4.fieldNote: The longer timeline eases her because her children would be grown, which is what makes the other pictures frightening. Her public line is to not panic, while privately she knows age and lack of qualifications still count against her. She spreads responsibility across government, companies and individuals, in a typically middle-ground way.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Sam and me both out, no time and no money, and the kids in the middle. What would help is somebody teaching people like me in person, slowly, on a real job, and enough money to keep the house while we learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about small firms like Gerry's. Everyone talks about big companies, but most of the building round here is two or three people in a van. If they go, a whole town's worth of skills goes with them.

headlineQuote: Most of the building round here is two or three people in a van. If they go, a whole town's worth of skills goes with them.
portrait: Elena is a 43-year-old labourer and trainee carpenter at a three-person building firm doing extensions and loft conversions in a market town. She came to building after self-checkouts cut her supermarket hours, and her partner Sam picks orders in a warehouse that already uses robots. She avoids computers and wants only to learn a trade that's hers. She is calm in the plateau, uneasy in the steady picture, panicked by AGI in two years and less frightened as the timeline stretches and her children grow up. She blames no one in particular and thinks everyone shares responsibility.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and Sam would both lose their jobs with no time and no money, and the kids would be caught in the middle.
whatWouldHelp: Someone teaching people like her slowly and in person on real jobs, and enough money to keep the house while they learn.
